claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite containing discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments in a Cu matrix.
Ni is a suitable low-melting alloying addition for inducing a transient liquid phase in W–Cu.
Rapid ultrahigh-temperature sintering with a minor Ni addition will induce a transient liquid phase at W–Cu interfaces.
Liquid-phase-assisted ultrahigh-temperature sintering can generate a crystalline intergranular phase upon cooling.
The proposed treatment will form a coherent interfacial layer between W and Cu.
The interfacial layer will bridge the W and Cu phases.
The transient liquid phase will enhance wetting at W–Cu interfaces.
The transient liquid phase will enhance interdiffusion between W and Cu.
Enhanced interfacial wetting and interdiffusion will reduce interfacial void formation.
Enhanced interfacial wetting and interdiffusion will inhibit phase separation in W–Cu.
A more continuous W–Cu interface will improve phonon and electron transport across the joint.
The Ni-assisted treatment will significantly improve thermal conductivity relative to an untreated W–Cu composite.
The thermal-conductivity improvement will persist after severe thermal cycling and irradiation.
Untreated W–Cu composites inherently suffer from phase separation and interfacial void formation.
Phase separation and interfacial voids cause poorer thermal performance in untreated W–Cu composites.
The intervention requires processing at a temperature sufficient to form the transient liquid phase.
The long-term stability of the proposed interfacial layer under prolonged service has not been established.
The quantitative thermal-conductivity improvement and robustness under extended irradiation and thermal cycling remain unknown.

contradictions.description: The predicted comparison is against an untreated W–Cu composite, whereas the experimental control receives the same ultrahigh-temperature sintering treatment but lacks Ni. This control isolates the Ni contribution but is not an untreated baseline.
